analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to order food recalls, shut down unsafe facilities, and police imported food.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2008 by Sen. Durbin with bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the FDA oversees the nation's food supply. It would require food facilities to identify hazards and put preventive controls in place, give the FDA power to force a recall (today recalls are voluntary), suspend the registration of facilities that make dangerous food, and inspect food imports more aggressively through foreign supplier verification. It would also fund this through fees on food facilities and importers, set safety standards for fruit and vegetable growing, improve disease outbreak tracking, and create voluntary food-allergy management guidelines and grants for schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers gain the most: the FDA could order a recall of contaminated food instead of asking a company to recall it voluntarily, shut down a facility producing unsafe food, and inspect imports based on risk rather than chance. Families with food-allergic children get federal guidelines and school grants for stocking epinephrine and training staff. Honest food companies also benefit modestly, since mandatory recalls and inspections apply to competitors who cut corners.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA mandatory recall authority: if a company refuses to voluntarily pull contaminated food, the Secretary can order distribution stopped, require notice down the supply chain, and mandate public notification of the recall.

Lets the FDA suspend a food facility's registration — shutting it out of interstate commerce and imports — when its food has a reasonable probability of causing serious health consequences or death, with a hearing within two days and a corrective-action plan required to reinstate.

Requires every registered food facility to conduct a hazard analysis, implement preventive controls, monitor them, keep records for two years, and make its written food-safety plan available to FDA inspectors.

Directs FDA to inspect facilities based on risk: every high-risk facility inspected at least once every two years at first, then annually, with an annual public report to Congress on what was and was not inspected.

Establishes science-based standards for growing and harvesting produce, foreign supplier verification and FDA inspection of foreign facilities that ship food to the U.S., and enhanced CDC foodborne-illness surveillance and traceback of raw agricultural commodities.
Directs FDA to finally issue the long-pending final rule on preventing Salmonella Enteritidis in shell eggs within one year of enactment.

Creates voluntary federal guidelines for managing food allergies and anaphylaxis in schools and early-childhood programs, plus grants of up to $50,000 a year to local school districts to buy epinephrine, train staff, and educate parents.

analysis.who_pays: Domestic food facilities and importers pay new fees for reinspections, recalls, and port-of-entry checks, plus the cost of hazard analyses, preventive-control plans, recordkeeping, and produce-safety standards. Small and very small businesses get two to three extra years before the preventive-controls rules apply. Schools pay a 25% local match if they take the allergy grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food facilities, importers, and produce growers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new fees on domestic food facilities and importers to pay for reinspections, recalls, and port-of-entry checks, and requires every registered facility to run a written hazard-analysis and preventive-controls program — compliance costs that fall hardest on small processors and that are likely to be passed to consumers in prices.

It lowers the evidentiary standard for administratively detaining food from 'credible evidence' to 'reason to believe,' and lets the FDA suspend a facility's registration and force a recall before a full hearing, which raises due-process concerns for businesses facing a de facto shutdown on an agency order.

Import safety rests heavily on foreign supplier verification and third-party auditors accredited under a new FDA registry, which shifts gatekeeping to private firms whose quality and independence can vary.

The bill's funding is fragile: fees can only be collected if FDA's food-safety appropriations grow at least 4.5% a year, otherwise they must be refunded, so the new inspection and enforcement program depends entirely on future appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill would have given the FDA tools the agency plainly lacked after years of high-profile outbreaks: the power to force a recall, shut down a dangerous plant, and check food at the border based on risk. The costs — fees on facilities and importers and preventive-control paperwork — are real but were phased in over two to three years for smaller firms and are capped by the bill. The main design weakness is money: fee collections are refundable unless FDA's own appropriations grow at least 4.5% a year, so the bill's enforcement strength ultimately depends on Congress actually funding the agency.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin (D-IL) introduced the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act on July 31, 2008, joined by an unusually bipartisan group of senators: Republicans Judd Gregg, Richard Burr, and Lamar Alexander and Democrats Christopher Dodd and Tom Harkin.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further steps of any kind: no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

The bill would have expanded FDA authority to regulate food, including power to suspend a food facility's registration and to order a stop-distribution or recall of food, and would have assessed fees on domestic food facilities and food importers.

The bill text requires facilities to analyze hazards and implement preventive controls, directs risk-based inspection of high-risk facilities at least annually, and creates produce safety standards, import verification programs, and school food-allergy guidelines and grants.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food facilities and importers avoided the bill's fees, preventive-control requirements, and expanded inspections for the two more years the old rules stayed in place. Consumers did not get the protections until a successor version passed the next Congress and became law in January 2011.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food facilities and importers that dodged new rules

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding support from a senator closely tied to agriculture.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the July 31, 2008 referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — so the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat, Dick Durbin, with 5 cosponsors of whom 3 were Republicans (Gregg, Burr, Alexander) and 2 Democrats (Dodd, Harkin); it died without a vote rather than along party lines.

industries.note: The bill requires preventive-controls plans, biennial registration renewal, risk-based inspections, and reinspection/recall fees capped at $25 million and $20 million a year. Industry bears real compliance costs, but a risk-based system also limits the damage that recalls and outbreaks inflict on the industry itself.

Importers face port-of-entry reinspection fees, foreign supplier verification requirements, and possible import certifications — the bill's answer to a food supply increasingly sourced abroad. Their interest in light-touch border checks runs against the public's interest in safe imports.

New science-based minimum standards for growing, harvesting, and storing fruits and vegetables — covering water, fertilizer, hygiene, and animal encroachment — would apply to growers, with compliance time adjusted for small businesses but no blanket exemption in this version.

industries.industry: Private testing labs and third-party auditors
industries.note: The bill creates an FDA registry of accredited bodies for food-testing laboratories and a system of accredited third-party auditors for import certifications, building a private quality-control sector alongside the public inspectorate.
